subject: Prior sensitivity/poorly unconstrained posteriors with bernoulli_logit, dummy variables and constant term

messages.author: 06b57f25e554a736
messages.subject: Prior sensitivity/poorly unconstrained posteriors with bernoulli_logit, dummy variables and constant term
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to figure out the behavior of a very simple bernoulli_logit model. I'm testing it with fake data. The data is N observations of bernoulli trials. The probability of success for each trial is inv_logit(a linear combination of the M features). The goal is to infer the posterior distribution of the coefficients of the linear combination:

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> M;
matrix[N, M] X;
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
}
parameters {
vector[M] beta;
}
model {
beta ~ normal(0, 2);
y ~ bernoulli_logit(X * beta);
}

This model works fine with continuous features drawn from a normal distribution. It also works fine with an additional feature of all-1s to provide the linear combination with a constant term. And it works fine with 3 features constructed by turning a categorical variable with 3 possibilities into 3 dummy variables (i.e. onehotencoding).

But if I use the dummy variables and a column of ones then the model becomes extremely prior sensitive, the posteriors change shape drastically, and are very wide.

And if I try the dummy variables and a column of ones without a prior on beta then the result is disastrous: the joint posterior distribution is essentially a very large plane, the marginalized distributions are multimodal, neff is very small, and the model takes 2 orders of magnitude longer to run.

Here's a notebook showing what I mean: https://gist.github.com/williamsmj/e164950c70dc3ed8d59206a0dcfbc57f.

I realize choice of prior is important, and not idiot-proof, but the very drastic effect of the combination of dummy variables and a constant term seems to me rather extreme.

Is the constant term redundant when the features include dummy variables? Or is something subtler going on?

Thanks,
Mike

parts:
> On Jul 7, 2016, at 2:15 PM, Mike Williams <mi...@mike.place> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I'm trying to figure out the behavior of a very simple bernoulli_logit model. I'm testing it with fake data. The data is N observations of bernoulli trials. The probability of success for each trial is inv_logit(a linear combination of the M features). The goal is to infer the posterior distribution of the coefficients of the linear combination:
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> N;
> int<lower=0> M;
> matrix[N, M] X;
> int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
> }
> parameters {
> vector[M] beta;
> }
> model {
> beta ~ normal(0, 2);
> y ~ bernoulli_logit(X * beta);
> }
>
> This model works fine with continuous features drawn from a normal distribution. It also works fine with an additional feature of all-1s to provide the linear combination with a constant term. And it works fine with 3 features constructed by turning a categorical variable with 3 possibilities into 3 dummy variables (i.e. onehotencoding).
>
> But if I use the dummy variables and a column of ones then the model becomes extremely prior sensitive, the posteriors change shape drastically, and are very wide.

Exactly as they should! What's happening with that one-hot encoding
is that you're overparameterizing and the model's likelihood is no
longer identifiable. I discuss the simplest possible case of this
in the manual chapter on problematic posteriors. The point is that
if beta[1] is your coefficient for the constant 1 and beta[2:K] are
your one-hot parameters, then

beta[1] + c, beta[2:K] - c

gives you the exact same likelihood.

The standard solution is to leave out one of the one-hot encodings.
That is, if it's a three-way variable, use the coding:

c = 1: x[1] = 1, x[2] = 0
c = 2: x[1] = 0, x[2] = 1
c = 3: x[1] = 0, x[2] = 0

You'll find discussions of this in many intro regression books.

With maximum likelihood, you need identifiable models. With Bayes,
you can put a prior on beta, which technically affords a proper posterior,
but that posterior's going to be heavily influenced by the prior, as one
might expect, because the prior's providing the identification. Again,
I discuss just this in the manual chapter on problematic posteriors.

- Bob

P.S. It's great that you did this. Simulation is a great way to
explore. We recommend everyone always do this for any model they
want to program in Stan.

Thanks for the manual pointers and the extremely clear elaboration for this special case!

I updated the notebook to demonstrate that this standard solution works beautifully (see the last two figures):

https://gist.github.com/williamsmj/1ed7b2bc805d8260f85b458865f71e72

And if I've understood things correctly, a hand-wavy way of explaining this might be...

 - the dummy variables always sum to 1 by definition, so together they effectively form a second intercept
 - this de facto second intercept induces the problems described in the manual (Collinearity of Predictors in Regressions)
 - but one of the dummy variables can be dropped without loss of information, such that the dummy variables no longer always sum to 1, and the problems go away :-)

Mike
